**Yes, the cable can cap your charging speed.** Charging runs at the lowest limit among the charger, the cable, and the device. A 100W charger on a 60W cable gives you 60W at most, and a 240W cable can't make a 65W laptop charge faster than 65W ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/cable_connector): a certified cable "does not augment the capabilities of" the products it connects).

**What the ratings mean**
- **60W cables** carry up to 20V at 3A. That's enough for most phones, tablets, and many thin laptops.
- **100W cables** carry 20V at 5A. They need an e-marker chip to tell the charger the cable can handle 5A.
- **240W cables** carry 48V at 5A (USB PD 3.1 EPR). The spec requires an e-marker, and the cable must carry the 240W logo ([UL Solutions](https://www.ul.com/insights/240w-usb-c-cable-performance-testing-and-safety-considerations)). The higher voltages (28V, 36V, 48V) give 140W, 180W, and 240W ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/usb-charger-pd)).

**A caveat on 100W:** USB-IF replaced the 100W USB-C cable category with 240W in its spec, and stopped certifying 100W cables on December 22, 2021. Officially, certified cables are now only 60W or 240W ([UL Solutions](https://www.ul.com/insights/240w-usb-c-cable-performance-testing-and-safety-considerations), [USB-IF compliance updates](https://compliance.usb.org/index.asp?Format=Standard&UpdateFile=Cables+and+Connectors&pubDate=20261005)). "100W" cables are still sold, but they're a marketing label for a 5A cable, not a USB-IF-certified tier.

**What to buy, by device**
- **Phone, tablet, or a laptop under about 60W:** any decent 60W cable is fine.
- **Laptop charging at 65–100W:** use a 5A e-marked cable (100W or 240W).
- **Laptop or dock above 100W:** you need a 240W cable, plus a charger and device that support EPR.

**One example for the 100W case:** the [Baseus USB-C to USB-C Cable, 100W](https://dealectric.com/go/baseus-usb-c-cable-100w) is $9.99 for 1 m ($12.99 for 2 m, $16.99 for 3 m) per the [listing](https://dealectric.com/baseus-usb-c-cable-100w). It's e-marked at 5A. Its limits are:
- It's USB 2.0 data only (480 Mbps).
- It has no video output.
- It isn't rated for 140W or 240W.
- Baseus says it isn't supported for iPad Pro charging.

The link is an affiliate link, so the merchant pays a commission at no cost to you.

**How to check a cable you already own**
- Look for a 60W or 240W logo on the cable or packaging. Certified cables must carry one.
- Cables with no markings are best treated as 60W or lower.
- If the wattage you see is lower than expected, try a different cable first, since it's the cheapest thing to swap.
